pool.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
pool.name: Personal & Professional Development
pool.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
pool.discipline: Academic writing
pool.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
pool.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
pool.contributionReview: Academic writing, research literacy and civic engagement; a valid required foundation, not religious-studies substance.

pool.description2: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.
pool.name: Calling Bullshit
pool.profile: Examines misinformation through philosophy, history, psychology and practical information evaluation. Students distinguish misleading discourse from related concepts, investigate cognitive and social vulnerabilities, and analyze pseudoscience, statistical misrepresentation and reasoning errors. Fact-checking, deepfake production and response exercises develop recognition and intervention skills. Projects map a misinformation narrative's actors and circulation and produce a research-grounded myth-debunking video with an external interview.
pool.discipline: Misinformation studies; Psychology; Applied epistemology; Science communication
pool.topics: Bullshit, lying and misinformation; Historical hoaxes and propaganda; Cognitive bias and motivated reasoning; Social identity and information overload; Scientific credibility and pseudoscience; Publication bias and misconduct; Misleading statistics and data displays; Reasoning fallacies; Deepfakes; Misinformation diffusion; Debunking and counter-narratives; Medical and climate misinformation
pool.methods: Source-credibility evaluation; Fact-checking protocols; Reasoning-fallacy detection; Critical analysis of statistical claims; Misinformation-network mapping; Deepfake video construction and analysis; Debunking-message design; Expert interviewing; Documentary-style explanatory video production
pool.contributionReview: Misinformation, pseudoscience, cognitive vulnerabilities and narrative investigation directly inform conspiracy analysis; no sustained study of spiritual movements or religious change.

pool.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
pool.name: Law, Society & Justice
pool.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
pool.discipline: Law; Socio-legal studies; Legal philosophy
pool.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
pool.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review
pool.contributionReview: Socio-legal reasoning and justice support public religion questions; general legal survey does not teach religious institutions.

pool.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
pool.name: Modern History
pool.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
pool.discipline: Modern history
pool.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
pool.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development
pool.contributionReview: Modernity, nationalism, empire and migration provide chronological context; does not establish a religious-change sequence.

pool.description2: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
pool.name: History of Empires
pool.profile: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.
pool.discipline: Global history; Imperial history
pool.topics: Concepts and theories of empire; Imperial rise, expansion and decline; Administration and succession; Military and economic structures; Imperial ideologies and legitimacy; Culture and empire; Ancient and medieval empires; European overseas empires; Modern Asian and Eurasian empires; American power; Contemporary and future empires; Imperial legacies
pool.methods: Comparative historical analysis; Historiographical analysis; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historical research-question development
pool.contributionReview: Comparative imperial legitimacy, ideology and culture support colonial contexts; no independent comparative religion coverage claimed.

pool.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
pool.name: Native American Histories
pool.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
pool.discipline: Indigenous studies; Social and cultural history; Public history
pool.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
pool.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production
pool.contributionReview: Indigenous histories, boarding schools, cultural resistance and collaborative knowledge are substantive for colonial heritage; religion-specific content beyond stated evidence is not assumed.

pool.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
pool.name: Researching the “American Century”
pool.contributionReview: Full historical inquiry, critical source engagement and a substantial paper make a genuine advanced research contribution. Official description receives full consideration; no Walcheren content or detailed religious specialism is inferred.

pool.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
pool.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
pool.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
pool.discipline: Human rights law; Legal philosophy; Ethics
pool.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
pool.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis
pool.contributionReview: Religious freedom among human-rights controversies is a direct legal contribution; the balance of the course is legal/philosophical human rights.

pool.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
pool.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
pool.profile: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.
pool.discipline: Comparative constitutional law; Administrative law
pool.topics: Constitutional origins and fundamental features; Federalism and decentralization; Parliaments and lawmaking; Governments and heads of state; Court systems and judicial review; Constitutional rights; EU constitutional order; Administrative-law functions; Public participation; Administrative remedies; Procedural fairness, discretion and legitimate expectations
pool.methods: Comparative constitutional analysis; Constitutional and legislative interpretation; Case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to hypothetical facts; Structured comparative legal writing
pool.contributionReview: Comparative constitutions, rights and stated religious constitutions contribute to state/religion analysis, without constituting broad study of religious life.

pool.description2: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
pool.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
pool.profile: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
pool.discipline: Philosophy; Epistemology; Ethics; Metaphysics; Philosophy of mind
pool.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life
pool.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development
pool.contributionReview: God, meaning and Buddhist self perspectives are genuine philosophical belief content; introductory range does not establish advanced comparative traditions.

pool.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
pool.name: Ethics
pool.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
pool.discipline: Moral philosophy; Metaethics; Practical ethics
pool.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
pool.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development
pool.contributionReview: Normative moral theories, death and meaning contribute to existential and care questions; no religious-text/ritual sequence.

pool.description2: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
pool.name: Philosophy of Mind
pool.profile: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. pool.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
pool.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
pool.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
pool.discipline: Ancient history; Archaeology; Classical studies; Political sociology
pool.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
pool.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design
pool.contributionReview: Myth, religion, ritual and Athenian political institutions directly integrate belief and public life; sustained in one historical context rather than comparative contemporary traditions.

Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
pool.name: Writing Art's Histories
pool.contributionReview: Art historiography, interpretation and global disciplinary methods support heritage research; no religion-specific methods inferred from description.

pool.discipline: Literary studies; Comparative literature; Literary criticism
pool.topics: Literature, canon and world literature; Epic and heroism; Tragedy, fate and identity; Autobiography and memory; Framed storytelling and narrative power; Gender and agency; Essay and philosophical tale; Satire and irony; Colonialism and its critique; Modernist narration and subjectivity; Alienation and family; Art, sexuality and civilization; Magical realism
pool.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration
pool.contributionReview: Epic, mortality and confessional writing support textual/worldview interpretation; general literary range does not replace study of sacred texts in religious practice.

pool.description2: Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures.
pool.name: World Myth & Literature
pool.profile: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
pool.discipline: Comparative literature; Classical studies; Mythology; Religious studies
pool.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses
pool.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation
pool.contributionReview: Comparative Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic, African and classical myths offer strong direct narrative/worldview content and myth theory; this is a real contribution, not complete lived-religion or social-methods training.

pool.description2: Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
pool.name: Film & Text
pool.profile: Studies the translation of literary narratives into film through formal analysis and adaptation theory. Students compare plot, structure, characterization and setting with cinematic image, acting, editing, music and sound. Medium specificity, fidelity, intertextuality, auteurism, heritage and adaptation markets frame theoretical debates. A substantial research project applies selected concepts to literary and film material, developing an independent interpretation and leading a text- and film-based discussion.
pool.discipline: Adaptation studies; Film studies; Literary studies
pool.topics: Literature-film relationships; Narrative and medium specificity; Fidelity debates; Cinematography and mise-en-scène; Editing, continuity and montage; Film music and sound; Intertextuality; Auteurism; Adaptation and heritage; Adaptation markets; Spectatorship and immersion
pool.methods: Formalist literary analysis; Close film-sequence analysis; Comparative text-film analysis; Intertextual analysis; Theory-led adaptation research
pool.contributionReview: Adaptation and cross-cultural narrative interpretation support religion/media questions as transferable analysis; no religious object guaranteed.

pool.description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.
pool.name: Introduction to Film & Media
pool.profile: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.
pool.discipline: Film studies; Media studies
pool.topics: Film form and meaning; Cinematography, editing and sound; Mise-en-scène, narrative and performance; Early cinema; German Expressionism and Soviet montage; Classical Hollywood and European New Waves; Feminist film theory; Postcolonial media; Blockbusters; Television and digital platforms; Representation and spectatorship; Media convergence
pool.methods: Close film and media analysis; Historical and cultural contextualization; Application of feminist and postcolonial film theory; Independent analytical or creative-analytical media research
pool.contributionReview: Representation, identity and feminist/postcolonial analysis support media context; no sustained religious-media content assumed.

pool.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
pool.name: Media Archaeology
pool.profile: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
pool.discipline: Media archaeology; Media history; Material culture studies
pool.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
pool.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research
pool.contributionReview: Material histories of communication and knowledge support transmission/heritage research; no specific religious knowledge sequence.

pool.description2: Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship.
pool.name: From T.V. to TikTok
pool.profile: Examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Storytelling, power and representation connect television, film and digital forms to conformity, identity and imagined futures. Students analyze 1950s media, compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, and investigate disability representation. Futures-oriented projects create a speculative television-episode proposal and imagine possibilities that center disabled people.
pool.discipline: Media studies; Social and cultural history; Disability studies; Futures studies
pool.topics: Media storytelling and power; American everyday life; 1950s television and conformity; Science fiction and social anxieties; Media futures and marginalization; Indigenous representation and self-representation; Disability stereotypes and visibility; Authentic voice and cultural agency; Future foresight and inclusive scenarios
pool.methods: Historical analysis of primary media sources; Comparative representation analysis; Future-foresight scenario development; Theory-based speculative narrative design; Disability-centered futures inquiry
pool.contributionReview: American media, conformity and Indigenous/disabled self-representation support identity questions; not current religious communities as defining content.

pool.description2: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
pool.name: Media & the Environment
pool.profile: Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations. Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.
pool.discipline: Environmental humanities; Media studies; Ecocriticism
pool.topics: Environmental representation; Anthropocene; Animal representation and human-nonhuman relations; Deep time and ecological temporality; Biocentrism and environmental justice; Contested ideas of nature; Indigenous and postcolonial media; Ecological risk and scientific knowledge; Environmental affect and perception; Agency, scale and responsibility; Sustainability discourse
pool.methods: Close film, image and sound analysis; Comparative analysis of media forms and representational strategies; Ecocritical interpretation; Theory-based analytical or creative media inquiry
pool.contributionReview: Environmental humanities, indigenous/postcolonial media and human-nonhuman representation support climate-worldview analysis; not religious traditions by presumption.

pool.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
pool.name: Media & Race
pool.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
pool.discipline: Cultural history; Media studies; Race and ethnicity studies; American studies
pool.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
pool.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection
pool.contributionReview: Racial construction, historical/media evidence, observation and Photo/Voice contribute to exclusion and identity analysis; religion-specific coverage remains unestablished.

pool.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
pool.name: The Documentary
pool.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
pool.discipline: Documentary studies; Film studies; Media production
pool.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
pool.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice
pool.contributionReview: Documentary modes include ethnography and ethical representation with practical production; valuable research communication, without substituting film production for religious studies.

candidateAttempts.label: Worldviews, public life & cultural heritage
candidateAttempts.concept: Examine how worldviews acquire meaning in texts and material culture and interact with public institutions, combining philosophical argument, myth, art/archaeology, rights and social inquiry.
candidateAttempts.limitation: This coherent combination offers substantial religion-related textual/material and philosophical encounters, especially African visual traditions and ancient democracy. It lacks sustained study of contemporary religious traditions, communities and change across the public-life questions central to this target. Generic methods can be applied to religion but cannot create the missing taught subject. Failure is material response, not title, religion-count quota or disciplinary-equivalence requirement.

candidateAttempts.label: Belief, media & public discourse
candidateAttempts.concept: Analyze belief, identity, misinformation and exclusion through sociology, rights, psychology, rhetoric and media, with myth and public-ritual history.
candidateAttempts.limitation: A coherent communication/social inquiry programme, but its defining content becomes general persuasion, misinformation, political institutions and representation. Actual alternate spiritualities, religious texts/practices and change remain mostly unstated applications rather than taught substance.

ucrReview.recombination: Adding current NativeAmerican/empire research, description-only AmericanCentury methods, social movements/environmentaljustice, climatecommunication, medicalpsychology or museum/art historiography strengthens contextual/research capacities. It does not supply missing sustained religious subject matter. Philosophy and myth already concentrated in strongest candidate; replacing useful media with more generic context cannot cure material shortfall. No third near-duplicate manufactured; no accepted first closest match, so additional-alternative distinctness gates have no active pair.
ucrReview.feasibilityBoundary: Concepts rejected on course substance before constructing active schedules. No offering blanks or absent later planning columns used to infer academic no-match. No active UCR courses, placements, comparison blocks or optional research column. Preserved historical48placements are not current schedule certification.
